newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Ocampo sees signs of recovery already.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Ocampo sees signs of recovery already.

text.p: Colombia's Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said Wednesday the economic slump in 1996 was not as bad as expected taken in the overall context of Latin America and said the green shoots of recovery were already appearing.

He said the growth in gross domestic product, 3.0 percent this year, would reach between 4.0 percent and 4.5 percent in 1997, stimulated by a mixture of policies including tight fiscal control, a devaluation of the peso against the dollar and low interest rates. In 1995, GDP growth was 5.28 percent.

"The growth rate for 1996 was positive if you compare it to the growth of other Latin American economies. It's not the lowest rate of the decade and we're already seeing signs of a return to more vigorous growth," Ocampo said.

He was speaking after the government's National Council for Economic and Political Planning gave an overview of 1996 economic performance and reaffirmed macroeconomic forecasts for 1997, first unveiled at the end of last month.
Ocampo said that 1997 growth could be higher than forecast if aggregate demand recovers and if private investment grows by 9 percent or more as predicted for next year.
"There will be a mixture of economic policies in 1997 -- fiscal control coupled with tight control on the value of the peso and low interest rates," Ocampo said.

Given higher-than-expected inflation in 1996 -- running at 20.76 percent to the end of November against the year target of 17 percent --coupled with a downturn in imports because of the economic slump, the government said after Wednesday's meeting that the deficit on the current account of the balance of payments dropped to 5.3 percent of GDP.
It was 5.5 percent in 1995. The balance of payments gap is forecast to drop further to 5.2 percent of GDP in 1997.
The deficit in 1996 was offset by the inflow of net foreign investment into Colombia, which totalled $2.6 billion.

The trade deficit fell in 1996 and was equivalent to 2.5 percent of GDP, compared to 3.4 percent the previous year. The government predicted the trade deficit ratio would remain at that level in 1997.

The deficit dropped on the back of a cut in imports as a proportion of GDP -- down to 19.5 percent compared to 20.4 percent in 1995. That figure is projected to fall further to 17.9 percent in 1997, the government said.
Exports made up 17 percent of GDP in 1996, against 17.3 percent the previous year. Exports as a proportion of GDP are projected to fall to 15.6 percent next year.
Highlighting some of the concrete impacts of the economic slump in 1996, Ocampo said the coffee industry -- a key export sector -- had been particularly hard hit.
The value of parchment coffee fell 14.6 percent in real terms, compared to 13.8 percent growth in 1995. Ocampo forecast the value of parchment coffee would increase 3.5 percent next year.
